scenes.narration: Twenty-five billion dollars. That is how much was traded on event contracts in America in March twenty twenty-six, according to the federal regulator. Contracts on elections, on interest rates, and above all, on sports games.
Here is the twist. The platforms that run these markets say they are not betting against you at all. They do not need you to lose. They just need you to trade.
So how does a market for hunches make money? And is it finance, or is it gambling?
By the end of this video, you will know how a yes-or-no contract works, where the fee hides, why most of the money is on sports, and why the courts cannot agree on what these markets are.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Start with the product. An event contract is a simple question with a yes or no answer. Will this team win tonight? Will the central bank cut rates next month? If the answer is yes, a yes contract pays one dollar. If the answer is no, it pays nothing.

Before the event, people trade these contracts at prices between zero and one dollar. If a yes contract trades at sixty-five cents, the crowd is saying, roughly, that the event has a sixty-five percent chance of happening. The price is the prediction.

And here is the key difference from a sportsbook. Kalshi, the largest of these platforms, says that you are always trading against another member of the platform, not the exchange itself. Someone buys yes. Someone else buys no. The exchange matches them in the middle.

That is why Kalshi calls itself an exchange, not a bookmaker. In twenty twenty, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the regulator that oversees futures markets, designated it as a contract market. The same kind of license that big futures exchanges hold.

keyframes.cue: designated it as a contract market
keyframes.label: items[1].at.cue

scenes.narration: Let me draw one contract. Here is the question. On the left, a buyer of yes, paying sixty-five cents. On the right, a buyer of no, paying thirty-five cents. Together, they put in one dollar. When the answer comes, one side takes the whole dollar. The exchange simply holds the money in between.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: So if the exchange never takes a side, where does its money come from?

keyframes.label: The exchange never takes a side…

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The answer is a toll. In its own words, Kalshi makes money by charging a transaction fee on the expected earnings on the contract. Not on who wins. On every trade, win or lose.

The formula it filed with the regulator in twenty twenty-two looks like this. Seven percent, times the number of contracts, times the price, times one minus the price. At a price of fifty cents, that works out to about one point seven five cents per contract, rounded up to the next cent. There is no fee when the contract settles.

keyframes.cue: At a price of fifty cents
keyframes.label: items[2].at.cue

scenes.narration: Notice the shape of that formula. The fee is biggest when the price is fifty cents, when the outcome looks like a coin flip. It shrinks near zero and near one dollar, when the result is almost certain. The platform earns the most on the questions people are least sure about.

Polymarket, its biggest rival, uses the same kind of formula for its American exchange. In a filing with the regulator, its rate for traders who take an existing offer rises to almost seven percent of the same price term. And traders who post offers and wait get a small rebate. Both platforms pay people to keep the market full.

Those people are called market makers. They post prices on both sides and, as Kalshi puts it, make money by collecting the spread. And Kalshi has said that one of its own affiliates trades on the exchange too, mainly as a spread trader. So the exchange itself is not your opponent, but the other side of your trade may be a professional.

Let me draw the toll curve. Along the bottom, the price, from zero to one dollar. Up the side, the fee. It starts near zero, climbs to its peak at fifty cents, and falls again. A hill, with the toll booth at the top, right where the hunches are most uncertain.

keyframes.cue: A hill, with the toll booth
keyframes.label: strokes[6].start.cue

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: A small toll on a huge number of trades adds up. And the biggest source of those trades is not politics.

…and the biggest source is not politics

scenes.narration: The platforms do not publish an official split. But the Pew Research Center analyzed data compiled by a crypto news site, The Block. In July twenty twenty-six, sports were the most traded topic on both platforms, by a large margin. By our calculation from that table, about four out of five dollars traded were on sports.

The growth claims are enormous, but they are claims. In October, Kalshi said its annualized trading volume now exceeds one trillion dollars, and that it handles over seventy-five percent of prediction market trading. It raised one billion dollars at a forty billion dollar valuation. None of those numbers is an audited figure.

Wall Street noticed. The company that owns the New York Stock Exchange, Intercontinental Exchange, said it would invest up to two billion dollars in Polymarket, at a valuation of about eight billion dollars before the investment.

And the sportsbooks joined in. DraftKings launched its own prediction product in December twenty twenty-five, with its own exchange and its own market maker. FanDuel launched one with CME Group, the giant futures exchange, in states where regular sports betting is not legal. The NBA named Kalshi and Polymarket its preferred prediction market exchanges.

Let me draw where the money goes. Here is one big circle, all the trading in July. Now cut it. A thin slice for politics, economics and everything else. And the rest, about four fifths, is sports. A market for hunches, mostly about who wins the game.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Which raises the obvious question. If it looks like sports betting, why is it not regulated like sports betting?

keyframes.label: If it looks like sports betting…

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The rules have not always been friendly. In twenty twenty-two, the regulator ordered Polymarket to pay a one point four million dollars penalty for running what it called an illegal unregistered facility. Then the climate changed. In July twenty twenty-five, the company that now operates as Polymarket US was designated as a regulated exchange.

Then the states pushed back. Sports betting in America is regulated by each state, with its own licenses and taxes. Several states told the platforms that their sports contracts were simply illegal bets. The platforms answered that they are federally regulated exchanges, and that states have no say.

The courts split. In April twenty twenty-six, a federal appeals court in the Third Circuit sided with Kalshi, two to one, at an early stage of the case. It said the sports contracts are swaps traded on a licensed exchange, under the federal regulator's exclusive control. One judge disagreed, and called that position a performative sleight.
Then in August, the Ninth Circuit, in a case from Nevada, went the other way. It said the contracts were not swaps, because they were sports bets. Two appeals courts, two opposite answers.

Now the question is knocking at the Supreme Court. New Jersey has asked the justices to take the case. As of today, they have not decided whether to hear it. Meanwhile, the federal regulator has taken the platforms' side. It dropped a plan to ban sports and political contracts, and it has sued several states.

Let me draw the tug of war. On one side, the platforms and the federal regulator, pulling toward finance. On the other side, the states and their gaming regulators, pulling toward betting. In the middle, the rope, a yes or no contract on tonight's game. And the referee has not blown the whistle yet.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: So whatever the courts decide, one part of this business is already clear.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Do the math on a single trade. You buy one hundred contracts at fifty cents, fifty dollars in total. Under the formula Kalshi filed, the fee is about one dollar and seventy-five cents. If you win, you collect one hundred dollars. If you lose, you get nothing. Either way, the toll was paid at the start.

For the whole market, the regulator put the numbers in perspective. Twenty-five billion dollars of event contracts in a month sounds huge. But it is about zero point zero eight percent of all the futures trading the commission oversees. Small for Wall Street, enormous for a product that barely existed a few years ago.

Let me draw the business model. On one side, thousands of traders with hunches. In the middle, the exchange, taking a small toll on every match. On the other side, the market makers, earning the spread. The traders win and lose against each other. The toll booth is the only one that collects on every single trade.

scenes.narration: So how do prediction markets make money off your hunches? Not by betting against you. By charging a small fee every time you trade, most of all when nobody is sure what will happen. Whether that makes them a financial market or a casino is a question the courts are still fighting over. But the toll booth gets paid either way.
